items.title: Prevalencia y factores asociados al síndrome de burnout en el personal de enfermería de instituciones hospitalarias: Búsqueda narrativa
items.abstract: Introduction: Burnout syndrome represented a relevant occupational health problem among nursing staff due to constant exposure to physical, emotional, and organizational demands. The objective was to analyze its prevalence in hospital institutions and identify the main occupational, personal, and organizational factors associated with its occurrence. Methodology: A narrative search of scientific literature was conducted in biomedical and nursing databases, emphasizing recent publications and systematic reviews addressing prevalence, associated factors, and consequences of burnout. The evidence reviewed showed variations in prevalence estimates according to populations, hospital services, measurement instruments, and work contexts. A review published in 2025 identified global prevalence rates of 33.45% for emotional exhaustion, 25.0% for depersonalization, and 33.49% for low personal accomplishment. Results: The main associated factors were work overload, long working hours, shift work, time pressure, lack of organizational support, role conflicts, and occupational stress. Greater vulnerability was identified in high-demand areas, such as emergency departments and intensive care units. Burnout was also associated with physical and mental health problems, absenteeism, staff turnover, and reduced quality and safety of patient care. Conclusions: Burnout syndrome constituted a multifactorial problem that affected nursing staff well-being and the quality of hospital services. Prevention and early detection, together with improvements in working conditions, shift organization, communication, and institutional support, were considered essential to reducing associated factors and promoting safe patient care.

items.title: Prompting Depth as a Behavioural Proxy for Cognitive Engagement: A Learning Analytics Study of Student–Chatbot Dialogues in EFL Writing
items.abstract: Cognitive engagement shapes learning but resists direct observation, and the spread of generative-AI chatbots in EFL writing has made post hoc self-reports even harder to trust. This study asks whether the depth of a learner’s prompts (their specificity, elaboration, metacognitive framing, higher-order quality, and iterative refinement) can serve as a behavioural trace of that engagement. Using the RECIPE4U dataset (1,913 prompts from 130 EFL learners), two coders scored three prompt-level dimensions with substantial to near-perfect agreement (κ = .74–.84); the remaining dimensions were derived from intent annotations and session structure. The five dimensions did not behave as one construct. At the student level, only elaboration correlated with essay revision (r = .34) and, weakly, with satisfaction (r = .20); metacognitive framing and higher-order request added little, and iterative refinement related negatively to revision (r = −.18). An equal-weight composite showed no association with either criterion (r = .07). Each one-point increase in prompting depth was associated with more than twice the odds of subsequent revision (OR = 2.37; course-adjusted OR = 2.09), an association that persisted in a random-intercept model despite marked between-student variance (ICC = .41). Prompting depth is best read dimension by dimension: elaboration, not depth in the aggregate, tracks revision-oriented engagement.

items.title: Psychometric Evaluation of Situation Awareness and Workload Measures in a Nuclear Microworld Simulation
items.abstract: The increasing automation of nuclear power plants introduces novel demands on operator situation awareness and workload management. Yet, commonly used measures of situation awareness and workload often lack comprehensive validation within nuclear contexts. This study evaluates four prominent measures: two of situation awareness (3D SART and SACRI) and two of workload (NASA-TLX and a secondary task performance metric) according to key psychometric criteria for nuclear control room simulations. Using the Rancor Microworld platform, twenty-six participants completed both routine and abnormal scenarios under different automation levels, following a within-subjects design. SACRI correlated with generated revenue and task time, NASA-TLX correlated with temperature management and number of actions, and secondary task performance correlated with task time; 3D SART showed no correlations. Predictive analyses showed that these relationships largely disappeared when automation level and scenario type were included as covariates. Sensitivity to experimental conditions varied across measures, with 3D SART and NASA-TLX affected by automation level, and NASA-TLX, SACRI and secondary task performance by scenario type. Measures were not redundant, and all demonstrated moderate reliability across experimental conditions. Findings provide insight to researchers and nuclear practitioners for selecting situation awareness and workload assessment tools and strengthening the technical basis for designing safer and more effective control room systems.

items.title: QUALIDADE DE VIDA E ESTRESSE OCUPACIONAL EM AGENTES COMUNITÁRIOS DE SAÚDE NA ATENÇÃO PRIMÁRIA À SAÚDE
items.abstract: O estresse ocupacional e a qualidade de vida no trabalho constituem aspectos relevantes para a saúde dos Agentes Comunitários de Saúde (ACS) e para a organização da Atenção Primária à Saúde. Este estudo observacional, de abordagem quantitativa e delineamento transversal, descritivo e correlacional, teve como objetivo analisar esses constructos entre ACS do município de Santa Luzia, Paraíba, e investigar a associação entre eles. A pesquisa contou com 35 participantes, que responderam a um questionário sociodemográfico e profissional, a um instrumento de qualidade de vida no trabalho fundamentado no modelo de Walton e à Escala de Estresse no Trabalho. Os dados foram analisados por meio de estatística descritiva e correlação de Spearman. Os resultados evidenciaram nível elevado de estresse ocupacional e avaliação desfavorável da qualidade de vida no trabalho, com médias de 3,84 e 2,38, respectivamente. Identificou-se associação negativa e estatisticamente significativa entre os constructos, especialmente nas dimensões condições de trabalho e trabalho e espaço total de vida. Conclui-se que melhores condições laborais e maior equilíbrio entre trabalho e vida pessoal são aspectos importantes para a qualidade de vida dos ACS, destacando-se a necessidade de ações institucionais voltadas à valorização profissional, ao suporte organizacional e à promoção de ambientes de trabalho saudáveis.

items.title: Recursive Adversarial Engine: A Closed-Loop Cognitive Safety Framework for Autonomous AGI Evolution
items.abstract: Large language models are approaching general-purpose capability, yet three failure modes—hallucination, ethical misalignment, and cognitive rigidity—continue to block reliable deployment, and existing defenses address them only reactively at the output level. This paper presents the Recursive Adversarial Engine (RAE), a cognitive-safety infrastructure that treats contradiction as a source of negative entropy and organizes defense as a five-stage closed loop: definition, adversarial engagement, iterative verification, convergence, and ethical fusing. RAE formulates model self-correction as a recursive fixed-point problem, quantifies cognitive quality through topological metrics, distributes adversarial pressure across a pool of heterogeneous agents, and enforces ethical boundaries through dual-layer circuit breakers. A system specification and internal deployment observations indicate that the design targets self-referential vulnerability false-alarm rates below 1%, consensus variance at or above ln(2), and parallel adversarial pools exceeding 100 agents. We compare RAE with conventional filtering, instruction tuning, and static red teaming, and discuss the framework's theoretical status, evaluation limitations, and deployment requirements for high-stakes domains.

items.title: Researcherly Dispositions and Teachers’ Artificial Intelligence TPACK Development: A Two-Wave Repeated Cross-Sectional Study of Adult Intellectual Development
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming classroom teaching, yet two-wave repeated cross-sectional evidence on how K-12 teachers develop the knowledge that underpins intelligent performance with AI remains scarce. Our two-year study across 29 schools thus explored the associations between university-facilitated teacher action research and the development of artificial intelligence technological pedagogical and content knowledge (AI-TPACK), a domain-specific form of intelligence-as-knowledge in teaching. Data were collected using questionnaires on research-related dispositions and AI-TPACK with 285 participants in Year 1 and 200 participants in Year 2. Structural equation modeling suggested that the associations of teachers’ research consumption and production with their AI-TPACK differed between the two waves, possibly reflecting shifting program task requirements, whereas research attitude served as a stable predictor. The findings yield preliminary evidence regarding linkages between action research and teachers’ AI-TPACK, and highlight the differences in these associations across the two waves. Considered from the perspective of adult intellectual development, these results suggest that knowledge in professional practice might be sustained by opportunities to convert inquiry into produced knowledge, refining accounts of how expertise with intelligent technologies develops.

items.title: Same rules, mixed messages: exploring community perceptions of academic dishonesty in computing education
items.abstract: Academic dishonesty has long been a concern in computing education, and the rapid growth of online learning and generative artificial intelligence (AI) has further complicated how cheating is perceived and addressed. We report on a study examining how different actors in the computer science (CS) classroom interpret potential cheating scenarios and the motivations behind academic dishonesty. Participants included instructors (n = 6), teaching assistants (TAs; n = 22), and undergraduate students (n = 538) enrolled in two CS courses at a large Southeastern institution in the United States. Respondents classified scenarios as serious cheating, trivial cheating, or not cheating and responded to an open-ended question about motivations for academic dishonesty. Our findings reveal differences in perceptions across the three stakeholder groups. Among the instructors who participated, grade pressure and laziness were the most frequently mentioned motivations for academic dishonesty, whereas students and TAs more frequently emphasized gaps in prerequisite knowledge and time management challenges. Given the small instructor sample, these qualitative findings should be interpreted as descriptive and exploratory rather than representative of instructors more broadly. These results highlight differences in how academic dishonesty is understood across classroom stakeholders and underscore the need for clearer communication of academic-integrity expectations and instructional strategies that help students interpret and navigate those expectations in computing education, particularly in post-COVID learning environments where hybrid instruction, increased reliance on digital resources, and AI-assisted tools have reshaped students’ approaches to coursework and learning.

items.title: Social Influence in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Preference for Humans Does Not Deter Artificial Intelligence Influence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming a source of social influence. But people often prefer human over AI sources (algorithm aversion/preference for humans), which might prevent AI from influencing humans. However, we outline a theoretical framework that suggests that preferences do not play a causal role in influence. To test this framework, we investigated under which conditions preferences predict AI influence. Participants (N = 1,254) indicated their adviser preference and then made incentivised decisions while receiving advice from AI or human advisers. Participants preferred human over AI advisers but were influenced by AI and humans similarly. A strong aversion to AI advisers had no (Study 1) or a trivial relation (Study 2 and 3) with AI influence, which was explained by confounding variables. When manipulated, preferences did not predict advice-taking, but adviser trustworthiness and competence did (Study 3). Our results suggest that for predicting AI influence, understanding domain-specific social cognitions, not preferences, is critical.

items.title: Spanning boundaries in socio-technological transformation: practical approaches for developing and iterating shared mental models
items.abstract: This article in the journal Gruppe. Interaktion. Organisation. (GIO) examines how organizations can intentionally develop, maintain, and continuously adapt shared mental models (SMMs) across team, functional, and hierarchical boundaries. Whereas prior research has primarily investigated the characteristics, measurement, and effects of SMMs within teams, comparatively less is known about how shared cognitive orientations emerge and can be cultivated within heterogeneous organizational and socio-technological networks. This question is particularly relevant to socio-technological transformation and human-AI collaboration, where divergent professional perspectives, technological systems, and evolving task allocations intensify the need for cognitive alignment. Based on a structured narrative literature review, the paper conceptualizes SMMs as boundary spanning cognitive infrastructures and derives overarching enabling conditions and five principles for their development and maintenance. Leadership, organizational culture, and psychological safety provide the necessary enabling conditions. Joint situational analysis, visual and scenario-based co-construction, and interdisciplinary skill profiles and shared language support SMM development. Iterative feedback loops and the deliberate unlearning of outdated assumptions enable their continuous adaptation. Actor-Network Theory complements this perspective by explaining how shared understandings emerge through translation, are mediated by material and digital artefacts, and become stabilized within socio-technical networks. The paper thereby extends SMM research toward an organization-wide and process-oriented perspective and provides actionable guidance for managing socio-technological transformation.

items.title: Strategi Inovasi Pendidikan Berkelanjutan Berbasis Kecerdasan Buatan dan Transformasi Digital dalam Membangun Kompetensi Generasi Muda Berwawasan Lingkungan
items.abstract: Perkembangan kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence/AI) dan transformasi digital telah membawa perubahan dalam penyelenggaraan pendidikan serta membuka peluang untuk menciptakan pembelajaran yang lebih adaptif dan inovatif. Namun, pemanfaatan teknologi dalam pendidikan perlu diintegrasikan dengan prinsip pembangunan berkelanjutan agar mampu mendukung pengembangan kompetensi generasi muda yang memiliki kepedulian terhadap lingkungan. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk menganalisis strategi inovasi pendidikan berkelanjutan berbasis kecerdasan buatan dan transformasi digital dalam membangun kompetensi generasi muda berwawasan lingkungan. Penelitian ini menggunakan metode Systematic Literature Review (SLR) dengan pendekatan deskriptif kualitatif. Pengumpulan data dilakukan melalui penelusuran, pemilihan, dan pengkajian artikel jurnal ilmiah yang relevan, kemudian dianalisis melalui tahapan identifikasi, pengelompokan, perbandingan, dan sintesis temuan berdasarkan fokus penelitian. Hasil kajian menunjukkan enam aspek utama dalam inovasi pendidikan berkelanjutan, yaitu transformasi digital sebagai fondasi pembelajaran adaptif, pemanfaatan AI untuk mendukung personalisasi dan efisiensi pembelajaran, penguatan kompetensi pendidik, integrasi Education for Sustainable Development (ESD), penerapan pembelajaran kontekstual berbasis Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) dan Project-Based Learning (PjBL), serta pengembangan kompetensi generasi muda. Hasil kajian juga menunjukkan bahwa penggunaan AI secara berlebihan berpotensi mengurangi keterlibatan peserta didik dalam proses berpikir sehingga diperlukan penguatan literasi digital dan kemampuan berpikir kritis. Dengan demikian, inovasi pendidikan berkelanjutan perlu mengintegrasikan teknologi, kompetensi pendidik, dan pendekatan pembelajaran yang berorientasi pada keberlanjutan untuk mendukung terbentuknya generasi muda yang kritis, kreatif, adaptif, serta memiliki literasi dan kepedulian lingkungan.

items.title: Structural Intelligence: Consolidated Research Corpus and Source Archive (2026)
items.abstract: This repository presents the consolidated research corpus of Structural Intelligence (SI), an interdisciplinary theoretical framework developed by Vladisav Jovanović within the broader research program of the Philosophy of Structure. The collection reorganizes 27 original publications into seven integrated manuscripts: Coherence, Contact, and Answerability; The Architecture of Correction; Evidence-Constrained Interpretation; Structural Debt; Structural Capture; Organization and Adaptation; and Wisdom Under Pressure. Together, these manuscripts examine the relationships between coherence, evidence, warranted correction, adaptive organization, human agency, and the distribution of unresolved costs. They situate the framework in relation to established research in epistemology, cognitive psychology, cybernetics, systems theory, enactivism, organizational learning, resilience engineering, and artificial intelligence evaluation. Structural Intelligence is presented as an integrative conceptual framework with testable research hypotheses, rather than a universal causal theory or a validated psychometric construct. The repository preserves the original manuscripts, revised consolidated publications, source inventories, content-preservation documentation, and SHA-256 checksums. Editable manuscript sources and supporting materials are included where available. Its purpose is to reduce bibliographic fragmentation while preserving the intellectual development, provenance, and conceptual contributions of the original research. The collection provides a coherent foundation for subsequent theoretical development, independent evaluation, and empirical investigation.

items.title: The Association of Behavioral Intention to Use Artificial Intelligence with Entrepreneurial Alertness and Intention Among University Students
items.abstract: The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) has increased interest in understanding individuals’ intention to use AI. However, little is known about how this intention is related to entrepreneurial alertness (EA) and entrepreneurial intention (EI). This study examined the relationships among behavioral intention to use AI (BI-AI), EA, and EI among university students in Türkiye. It also explored whether trait competitiveness (TC) and family entrepreneurial background (FB) moderate the relationship between EA and EI. Data were collected from 355 participants through an online cross-sectional survey. The measurement model was evaluated using confirmatory factor analysis together with reliability and validity assessments. PROCESS macro analyses with bootstrap confidence intervals were then used to test the proposed direct, indirect, and moderating relationships. The results showed that BI-AI was positively related to EA (b = 0.111, SE = 0.029, 95% CI [0.054, 0.167]). However, no significant direct relationship was found between BI-AI and EI (b = −0.017, SE = 0.078, 95% CI [−0.170, 0.135]. EA was positively related to EI (b = 1.136, SE = 0.142, 95% CI [0.857, 1.414]). The indirect relationship between BI-AI and EI through EA was also significant (b = 0.126, SE = 0.060, 95% CI [0.026, 0.256]). In the moderation analysis (N = 351), trait competitiveness significantly moderated the relationship between EA and EI (b = 0.231, SE = 0.060, 95% CI [0.113, 0.348]). Family entrepreneurial background, however, did not significantly moderate this relationship (b = −0.203, SE = 0.140, 95% CI [−0.478, 0.073]). The data indicate that EA may be relevant to understanding the link between BI-AI and EI and that the association between EA and EI is stronger among those with higher levels of TC. Because the study relied on cross-sectional data, the results should be interpreted as statistical associations rather than proof that one condition causes another. Future longitudinal and intervention-based research may provide a better understanding of how BI-AI, EA, and EI evolve over time.

items.title: The Cognitive Dimension of Complexity: On the Limits of Formalization and the Development of Cognitive Capabilities in the Age of AI
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) automates work for which established methods of problem formulation and solution already exist, the ability to act where such methods do not yet exist or no longer apply becomes relatively more valuable. This paper examines a cognitive dimension of complexity arising from the relationship between the properties of the reality under investigation and the cognitive capabilities of the subject (an individual or a team). Even before a problem is explicitly formulated, the language used to describe a real situation can introduce distortions. Three types of difficulty are distinguished by what must change: the model, the problem space, or the cognitive capabilities of the subject. AI can reinforce existing limitations as well as help reveal them; the outcome depends on how human–AI interaction is organized. The paper outlines a research agenda for Complexity Lab in which interaction with reality under incomplete knowledge may itself become a mechanism of cognitive development. It is addressed to leaders in business, engineering, and applied science.

items.title: The Price of Progress
items.abstract: This multidisciplinary perspective paper examines the rise of artificial intelligence, robotics and automation and their potential effects on human employment and livelihood. The paper considers technological progress from economic, psychological, social, philosophical, ethical and religious perspectives. It explores how automation may transform employment in hospitality, manufacturing, transportation, retail, administrative work and other sectors while also considering the new forms of employment that technological development may create. Particular attention is given to the human consequences of involuntary job displacement, including financial insecurity, identity, dignity, psychological wellbeing and economic inequality. The paper also examines the responsibilities of technology developers, employers, governments, workers and consumers during periods of technological transition. A distinctive part of the discussion considers Islamic concepts of justice, Rizq, human responsibility and the supplication of the oppressed in relation to technological displacement. This religious discussion is presented as ethical analysis and does not constitute a formal Islamic legal ruling or fatwa. The paper ultimately argues for human centred automation, in which technological progress is evaluated not only by efficiency and productivity but also by its contribution to human dignity, security and wellbeing. This is a perspective paper based on secondary research and personal interpretation. It does not present original experimental or survey data.

items.title: THE ROLE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHING
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an increasingly important component of modern education, particularly in the field of English language teaching. The integration of AI-powered educational technologies creates new opportunities for improving language acquisition, developing communicative competence, and providing individualized learning experiences. This article examines the role of artificial intelligence in English language teaching, focusing on its potential to enhance the four fundamental language skills: listening, speaking, reading, and writing. The study explores the pedagogical advantages of AI-based tools, including personalized instruction, automated feedback, adaptive learning, and increased learner motivation. Furthermore, it considers the challenges associated with AI integration, such as technological dependence, limited digital literacy, data privacy, and the importance of maintaining the teacher's professional role. The article emphasizes that artificial intelligence should be regarded as a supportive educational instrument rather than a replacement for human teachers. The effective implementation of AI requires a balanced approach that combines technological innovation with pedagogical principles and learner-centred instruction.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Multidisciplinary Tumor Boards for Breast Cancer: A Critical Review
items.abstract: Multidisciplinary tumor boards (MTBs) are the gold standard for breast cancer (BC) treatment planning, but rising caseloads and the growing number of clinical, pathological, and molecular factors under consideration are straining their capacity. AI, particularly large language models (LLMs), has been proposed as a decision support tool, and BC is the tumor type for which AI-MTB concordance has been studied most. We conducted a narrative critical review of studies comparing AI-generated treatment recommendations with breast MTB recommendations, along with evidence on MTB performance, earlier rule-based decision support systems, and the relevant regulatory and medico-legal environment. We evaluated 17 LLM studies published between 2023 and 2026. Overall concordance ranged from 16% to 94%, increasing with model generation, structured input, and guideline grounding, and decreasing with disease stage and case complexity. Concordance was consistently high for endocrine therapy and standard indications for systemic therapy, variable for surgery, radiotherapy, and genomic testing, and low or inconsistent for genetic counseling, anti-HER2 regimen selection, and the management of metastatic disease. Reproducibility was poor, and no study examined patient outcomes. Concordance with the MTB is not equivalent to clinical correctness, and hallucinations, the handling of incomplete information, and automation bias are distinct safety dimensions that concordance does not capture; we therefore propose a multidimensional evaluation framework. The current, limited evidence base supports using AI as a supervised, guideline-grounded pre-MTB tool in treatment planning rather than as a replacement for the MTB itself.

items.title: The stock market hallucination paradox: explanation depth, conversational naturalness and epistemic trust in GenAI assistants
items.abstract: Purpose – This study examines how the explanation depth and conversational naturalness of generative AI (GenAI) stock assistants relate to retail investors' perceived epistemic trust, perceived control, continuance intention and self-reported value co-creation, and how hallucination risk, overload and literacy condition these associations. Design/methodology/approach – Drawing on cognitive appraisal and epistemic trust theories, a cross-sectional survey of 386 Indonesian retail investors was analyzed with PLS-SEM, Gaussian copulas, PLSpredict, CVPAT and importance–performance map analysis (IPMA). Findings – Both design features were positively associated with trust and control, which were associated with continuance and co-creation. Perceived hallucination risk strengthened the explanation depth–trust association but weakened the naturalness–trust association. Overload was negatively related to control without significantly moderating the design features. Literacy moderated the trust–outcome associations in opposite directions. The explanation depth–control path was not robust to endogeneity correction. Research limitations/implications – The cross-sectional, self-reported, single-country design precludes causal inference; trust calibration against actual AI accuracy was not assessed. Practical implications – Providers could prioritize verifiable, layered explanations over conversational polish; regulators could consider disclosure and verification-literacy guidance. Originality/value – The study introduces perceived stock data hallucination risk as a context-specific construct and links perceived trust and self-reported engagement to managerial priorities.

items.title: The times they are AI-changin: my personal experience with artificial intelligence
items.abstract: I chronicle a new, unique paradigm shift at the intersection of human creativity and generative artificial intelligence. Following my retirement, I engaged the large language model Google Gemini as a digital co-pilot for my administrative and scientific activities. What began as a tool for basic text formatting, rapidly evolved into a sophisticated, synergistic collaboration, culminating in the co-authorship of a quantitative scientific manuscript in the field of “cultural musicology”, a totally new field of investigation for me. Based on my experience, I explore the profound structural advantages of AI assistants over human counterparts, emphasizing twenty-four-hour availability, near-instantaneous manuscript synthesis, and rapid drafting capabilities. I present a stark, cautionary analysis regarding the inevitable proliferation of autonomous, potentially malicious digital entities. I foresee an imminent epidemic of scientific paper retractions driven by unverified or intentionally corrupted data, raising the dystopian prospect of an algorithmic enforcement class or digital containment firewalls. AI is here to stay but it should be strictly regulated to avoid or minimize the undesirable serious consequences in science.

items.title: Theory of human–machine co-creation
items.abstract: Humans have long used machines to support creative work. Generative artificial intelligence has expanded opportunities for human–machine co-creation, in which computational systems generate and refine propositions in interaction with humans. However, the mechanisms and operations underlying these interactions remain insufficiently understood. We therefore propose a theory of human–machine co-creation. Our premise is that the human and the machine each have a distinct concept space and a knowledge space of their own, and that co-creation proceeds through the assimilation and elaboration of concepts and knowledge from each other’s propositions within these spaces. The proposed theory defines the mechanisms of adoption, abortion, and adaptation in human–machine co-creation, explaining when, why, and how the collaborators, i.e., humans and machines, accept, reject, or transform each other’s propositions. It further articulates the operations through which new concepts and knowledge are generated. The theory offers an ontology and an epistemology for understanding how humans and machines collaborate, and provides a foundation for describing these interactions and predicting their creative outcome.

items.title: THINKING BEFORE PROMPTING: LINKING SPATIAL REASONING, CRITICAL THINKING AND GENERATIVE AI THROUGH THE SPARC FRAMEWORK
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) produced explanations, diagrams and worked solutions in seconds, which raised a pedagogical dilemma: better task completion did not show that learners had practised the reasoning needed for independent performance. This conceptual paper examined the intersection of spatial reasoning, scientific reasoning and critical thinking in AI-supported higher education. A focused, illustrative synthesis of research on spatial cognition, cognitive offloading, human-AI interaction and educational scaffolding identified a plausible mechanism of concern: when AI supplied both a representation and its interpretation, students could bypass the construction, transformation and checking of mental models. The paper distinguished supportive from substitutive offloading and proposed SPARC (Sketch, Predict, Audit, Reconstruct, Calibrate), a five-stage instructional sequence that preserved learner-generated spatial and causal reasoning while using AI as a fallible comparison partner. Two teaching vignettes from introductory physics, the vertical motion of a tossed ball and work and power in stair climbing, showed how the sequence could be implemented with brief written or visual artefacts and assessed with an illustrative rubric. Four falsifiable propositions and a feasible pilot design were formulated for classroom evaluation. SPARC was not presented as an empirically validated intervention, and the available studies did not establish that GenAI necessarily caused durable declines in critical thinking. The paper concluded that educational evaluation should examine unaided transfer, reasoning quality and confidence calibration, rather than the quality of AI-assisted products alone.

items.title: Toward a relational model of subtle leadership: Referent power as the core mechanism of influence
items.abstract: Leadership scholarship continues to evolve amid complex organizational environments shaped by globalization, technological acceleration, workplace and workforce diversity, and heightened ethical expectations. While dominant paradigms emphasize visible behaviors and performance-oriented exchanges, leadership may also emerge through subtle relational mechanisms. This exploratory study examines Subtle Leadership, originally comprising seven dimensions (intrinsic motivation, authenticity, emotional intelligence, empowerment, integrity and trustworthiness, intuition, and referent power), and evaluates a refined model positioning referent power as the core mechanism of influence, predicted by the other six dimensions. Survey data from a consulting organization included colleague ratings of leaders (n = 49), team members (n = 45), and self-ratings from leaders (n = 5) and team members (n = 9). The newly developed instrument was analyzed using Cronbach’s alpha, exploratory principal component analysis, correlations, sequential and multiple regression, and Mann–Whitney U tests. Referent power demonstrated excellent reliability and the most coherent component structure, while other dimensions showed greater overlap and weaker item-level support. The six dimensions explained 64% of referent power variance among leaders and 79% among team members. Authenticity was the most consistent predictor, followed by empowerment, particularly among team members. Intuition correlated moderately with referent power but added no independent explanatory value. Self- and colleague assessments showed no significant differences. Given the small samples, findings neither confirm the original multidimensional structure nor establish a higher-order latent structure, but suggest an internally grounded relational model with referent power as the core mechanism of influence.

items.title: Toward AI leadership: A systematic literature review of leadership behaviors enacted by conversational agents in psychosocial interventions
items.abstract: This project is a systematic literature review that investigates how conversational agents (CAs; e.g., chatbots and virtual assistants) enact leadership-equivalent behaviors in psychosocial interventions, including therapy, counseling, and coaching. Advances in artificial intelligence have enabled these systems to move beyond process automation and engage in adaptive, relational, and motivational dialogue with users. As such, they increasingly perform functions that parallel those of human leaders, raising important theoretical and practical questions about the nature of leadership when enacted by nonhuman agents. The review has three main purposes. First, it examines which leadership behaviors are effectively exhibited by conversational agents, using Yukl et al.’s (2012) taxonomy of task-, relationship-, change-, and externally-oriented behaviors as an organizing framework. Second, it investigates the mechanisms through which these behaviors exert influence on users in psychosocial contexts, and identifies points of divergence from human-enacted leadership theory. Third, it distills methodological lessons from the existing evidence base, particularly regarding causal trustworthiness, intervention transparency, and replicability, to inform the design of future AI leadership research. The evidence base for this review draws primarily from rigorous experimental and longitudinal studies in medical and behavioral sciences, which provide a strong foundation for assessing agent-enacted influence. Synthesizing this literature, we aim to deliver: - An integrative behavioral framework that maps agent behaviors to leadership theory. - A research agenda outlining methodological standards and open questions for studying AI leadership. - Theoretical refinements that extend leadership theory to account for influence processes enacted by artificial agents. The expected outcome is a comprehensive and causally trustworthy assessment of how conversational agents perform leadership functions in psychosocial interventions, contributing both to leadership theory and to the responsible design of AI systems that increasingly shape workplace interactions.

items.title: Transformative Digital Practices for Social Equity: A Study of AI Adoption in Healthcare Through the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission for a Future-Ready Society
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used to support medical diagnosis, clinical decision-making, patient monitoring and the management of healthcare services. In India, the potential of these technologies must be considered alongside the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), which seeks to create an interoperable digital health ecosystem. This paper examines whether the adoption of AI can contribute to social equity in healthcare and what institutional, managerial and legal conditions are necessary for that contribution to be realised. It combines a review of selected academic and policy literature, an examination of the Indian legal framework and a small exploratory questionnaire study involving 19 medical professionals working in different healthcare settings. The survey findings indicate that respondents generally perceived some improvement in work efficiency, while also identifying patient data privacy, algorithmic bias, accountability, limited skills, technical support, and system integration as important concerns. The small sample does not permit national generalisation; rather, it provides an exploratory account of professional experience. The paper argues that ABDM should be understood as digital public infrastructure that may enable responsible data use, not as proof that AI has been uniformly adopted across the health system. It concludes that AI-enabled healthcare can advance social equity only when digital infrastructure is accompanied by clinical validation, human oversight, workforce development, inclusive access, privacy safeguards and clear accountability. The analysis is situated within the constitutional guarantees of equality, dignity, and privacy; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 and its phased commencement; applicable medical-device regulation; and relevant international guidance.

items.abstract: The emergence of artificial intelligence has brought positive and negative implications to the socio-economic lives of individuals.Whilst AI is one of the information communication technology tools, its utilisation and exploitation remain a source of contestation among People with disabilities.The major argument is how it will minimise the barriers created by disability.This study explores the views of those living with disabilities on the nature of opportunities that can be used to address the plight of those living with disabilities.The study adopted the qualitative approach, where purposively selected students and lecturers with disabilities responded to semi-structured interviews on the nature of their disability and what they think should be done to improve their plight.The case study design was adopted.Data from the interviews were thematically and content analysed.The findings revealed that People with disabilities look forward to artificial intelligence as a panacea and fortune to some of the barriers they encounter due to their disabilities.The study recommends that researchers should engage strongly with People with disabilities in order to come up with AI tools that can improve the livelihood of People with disabilities.

items.title: Trustworthy agentic AI systems: navigating the risks and governance of autonomous AI
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is evolving from the passive content generation of Generative AI (GenAI) to Agentic AI (AgAI) systems which are increasingly characterized by autonomy, adaptability, and goal-driven reasoning. Unlike traditional GenAI, AgAI systems are capable of perception, planning, and independent action. This shift introduces a unique class of sociotechnical risks, including goal misalignment, cascading operational errors, and security vulnerabilities. This paper reviews the AgAI landscape, examines its architectural components (planning, memory, action, and multi-agent collaboration) and its transformative potential across key sectors such as healthcare, education, manufacturing, robotics, and software development. By analyzing existing corporate and regulatory governance frameworks, the paper identifies gaps in accountability, liability, and real-time intervention. We argue that establishing trustworthy AgAI requires a shift from regulating content to constraining autonomous consequences, and propose seven research and governance challenges focusing on dynamic alignment, responsibility attribution, verifiable specifications, and standardized benchmarks, to ensure AgAI systems remain aligned with human values.

items.title: Undergraduate Students’ AI Readiness, Attitudes, and Perceptions of AI-Supported Learning: A Sequential Mixed-Methods Study in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in higher education, but little is known about how students’ readiness for AI relates to their evaluations of AI-supported learning, especially outside high-income settings. Using the Capability Approach as an interpretive lens, this sequential mixed-methods study examined undergraduates in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan. Interviews with 25 students preceded a survey of 497 students at eight universities, analyzed with structural equation modeling. All four self-reported readiness dimensions (cognition, ability, vision, and ethics) were positively associated with attitudes toward AI and perceived AI-enabled learning practices, which were associated with perceptions of AI-supported learning; five of 14 associations did not survive correction for multiple testing and are treated as tentative. The ethics associations were the strongest (β = 0.42) and most robust to common method variance. An exploratory model with direct paths fitted better, indicating misspecification of the hypothesized model. Interviews were consistent with the prominence of ethics, qualified other results, raised concerns about dependency, and suggested that access and institutional rules also shaped students’ use of AI. The cross-sectional, self-reported data support associational conclusions only. As a proposal for further examination, they suggest that ethical readiness may deserve a more central place in AI-related teaching and policy.

items.title: Understanding secondary school students’ attitudes toward artificial intelligence in education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) permeates all spheres of modern society, including the educational system, where it opens new possibilities for teaching and learning. This study examined the attitudes of secondary school students from Croatia ( N = 1394) toward AI, considering gender, place of residence, age, final academic achievement, parents’ education level, type of secondary school, and frequency of using AI-based applications. In addition to a sociodemographic questionnaire, the Student Attitude Toward AI (SATAI) scale [ 31 ] and the Attitudes Towards Artificial Intelligence Scale (ATTARI-12) [ 30 ], which measure the cognitive, affective, and behavioral aspects of attitudes toward AI, were used. The results confirmed that participants rated the factor related to the importance of integrating AI into the educational system the highest. Differences in attitudes toward AI were observed with respect to sex, type of secondary school, age, academic achievement, city size, and parents’ education. The results also confirmed significant differences in students’ attitudes toward AI according to the frequency of AI-based application use, with ChatGPT being the most frequently used AI tool among participants. Interestingly, socioeconomic factors were less strongly associated with students’ attitudes toward AI than the frequency of AI tool use was. This paper outlines the pedagogical implications of introducing AI into education, particularly in terms of structuring different approaches to integrating AI into the educational system.

items.title: Upgrading Humanity: The Future of Human Performance
items.abstract: Human performance has long been the preserve of elite athletes and executives with teams behind them. This paper argues that its definition is about to change, and that the change is a democratic one. Artificial intelligence now offers billions of people what only a few once had: answers, advice and the ability to offload cognitive work, at a price most can reach. Yet the upgrade is not landing. Today's devices measure people well and help them poorly. They hand their owners a second job: interpreting their own data. The paper proposes a new measure of performance, decision throughput: good decisions made and acted on for each unit of attention spent. On that measure, the next upgrade is not more data but fewer, better decisions left to the person, with the routine delegated to AI. Delegation depends on trust, and trust depends on control. Billions of people already show this every day in how they guard their phones. The paper sets out a trust loop and an architecture for a personal AI that works for its owner. Whether that becomes an upgrade for humanity or only for the affluent turns on one question: whether sovereignty reaches people where they already are, on their phones and in clouds they control.

items.title: Uso de inteligência artificial generativa no desenvolvimento de software: aplicações, benefícios e limitações
items.abstract: The advancement of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has transformed software development practices, expanding the possibilities for automation and support within software engineering activities. In this context, the adoption of this technology has garnered interest due to its impact on the productivity, quality, and security of the systems being developed. This article aims to analyze the primary applications, benefits, and limitations of generative artificial intelligence in software development. The methodology employed consists of a qualitative, descriptive literature review based on the analysis of scientific studies related to the topic. The investigation covers activities such as code generation, testing, debugging, maintenance, and system documentation. The analysis identifies contributions related to process optimization, task automation, and support for resolving technical problems. However, it also highlights limitations concerning the accuracy of responses, the reliability of solutions, and security risks. The study demonstrates that the impact of this technology varies depending on the context of its use and the specific nature of the activities being performed. It is concluded that generative artificial intelligence serves as a significant resource for supporting software development; however, its use requires human oversight and critical evaluation to ensure the quality and security of the resulting solutions.

items.title: Validation of the Chilean version of the Survey Work–Home Interaction Nijmegen
items.abstract: Background Work–family interaction is an important dimension of workers’ psychosocial health, as difficulties in reconciling work and family roles have been associated with adverse individual and organizational outcomes. Despite growing interest in this phenomenon, Chile lacks a validated instrument that captures its bidirectional nature and both its negative and positive dimensions. This study aimed to evaluate the psychometric properties of the Chilean version of the Survey Work–Home Interaction Nijmegen (SWING) among healthcare workers. Methods A sequential exploratory mixed-methods design was conducted. Content validity was first assessed through expert evaluation and review by end users. Subsequently, the psychometric properties of the instrument were examined in a sample of 1,011 healthcare workers from different regions of Chile. Analyses included exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, assessment of factorial stability across relevant subgroups, multigroup measurement invariance, internal consistency, convergent and discriminant validity, and validity evidence based on relationships with burnout. Results Findings supported the original four-factor structure of the SWING, comprising negative work-to-home, negative home-to-work, positive work-to-home, and positive home-to-work interaction. The factorial solution showed adequate fit and remained stable across gender, relationship status, caregiving responsibilities, and work setting. Configural, metric, and scalar invariance were supported across these groups. All four dimensions showed adequate internal consistency and evidence of convergent and discriminant validity. Associations with burnout were also consistent with the hypothesized relationships, providing additional validity evidence based on relationships with other variables. Conclusion The Chilean version of the SWING provided satisfactory evidence of validity, internal consistency, and measurement invariance among healthcare workers. The instrument provides a culturally appropriate measure for assessing both positive and negative work–home interactions in Chile and may support research, psychosocial risk assessment, and the development and evaluation of occupational health interventions aimed at improving work–life reconciliation.

items.title: What lies beneath the so-called “intelligent” AI computer models: A technical perspective on biases and AI use
items.abstract: This article explores the technical underpinnings of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to examine the societal implications of deploying AI in public policy and evaluation. The article starts with a lay presentation of the mathematical foundations of AI in general and particularly large language models (LLMs). It outlines how biases, often inherited from training data, are mathematically embedded deeply into the very architecture of the models. While AI excels in tasks with objective, well-defined outcomes, its use in domains requiring fairness, discretion, or cultural sensitivity poses significant risks. The article relies on real-world examples, such as Canada's immigration system, to discuss how algorithms can potentially amplify systemic inequities. The limitation of current bias mitigation tools, like fairness checklists or reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), is that they cannot fully address biases, particularly in high-stakes public sector uses. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential pitfalls of using generic pre-trained models for public policy and evaluation. For contexts demanding interpretive judgment or ethical accountability, AI should either be used for unambiguous tasks or avoided entirely. Ultimately, the integration of AI requires not just technical precision but democratic oversight, transparency, and context-sensitive design to safeguard equity and trust.

items.title: When AI Saves Time but Creates More Work: Digital Task Expansion and Employee Well-Being
items.abstract: Generative AI is sold as a time-saving technology, yet a growing body of workplace evidence describes people who use it and end up with more to do. This paper examines that contradiction through the idea of digital task expansion: the net growth in the tasks, scope and pace of a job that follows AI adoption, arising through verification and repair, learning and tool management, wider job scope and rising output expectations. It assembles published experiments, national surveys, a register-linked Danish study, an eight-month ethnography and the Gallup workforce panel (n = 21,648 in August 2026), and it applies secondary statistical analysis to the published tables. Time savings measured in the three positive controlled studies (12% to 40%) are roughly five times those measured in population surveys (2.8% to 5.4%), and one randomized trial found experienced developers 19% slower. Among frequent users in the Gallup data, time falls sharply for information gathering (net balance − 44 points) and writing (− 40) but not for reviewing and correcting work (− 2, 95% CI − 4.2 to 0.2) or learning new tools (+ 3, 1.0 to 5.0). Frequent users had nearly three times the odds of saying output expectations have risen (OR 2.95, 95% CI 2.60 to 3.36). In a 6,000-worker survey, frequent verification work rose from 35% of light users to 74% of heavy users. A break-even analysis shows that if overhead equals 58% of each hour saved and half of what remains is reabsorbed by wider scope, only 16% of users keep an hour a week free. The evidence is mostly self-reported and cross-sectional, so task expansion is treated here as a well-supported pattern and harm to well-being as a plausible, partly evidenced pathway. Organizations that measure freed time instead of tool use, and that protect context, quality standards and recovery, are best placed to avoid it.

items.title: When Does Valuing Meaningful Work Go Together with Job Satisfaction? Work Values, Job Characteristics and the Quality of Working Life in 47 Countries (ISSP 1989–2015)
items.abstract: Whether valuing meaningful work (work that is interesting, autonomous, helpful to others and useful to society) is good for workers' quality of working life is contested. Need-based accounts expect higher satisfaction; value–reward accounts warn of disappointment when work does not deliver; critical accounts see meaning as a privilege or a lever for exploitation. Using four waves of the ISSP Work Orientations module (1989–2015; 75,280 workers in 47 countries) and country × wave fixed effects, we find that workers who value meaningful work more are more satisfied with their jobs (β = 0.115 SD per SD), with both intrinsic–autonomy and prosocial components contributing. The association is specific to meaning-related values: the importance of security, income and advancement is not associated with satisfaction. And it runs through the job itself: once the perceived presence of interesting, independent and useful work is taken into account, valuing meaningful work is no longer associated with higher satisfaction, and where such work is lacking it even goes with somewhat lower satisfaction, the disappointment the value–reward account points to. The association does not differ measurably by education, power distance or long-term orientation; in the same countries it was stronger in 2015 than in 1997 and 2005. The three accounts thus describe complementary mechanisms rather than rival predictions. For quality-of-working-life research and practice, what matters is less whether people value meaningful work than whether their jobs provide it; meaning is no substitute for fair conditions.

items.title: When GenAI Increases Inequality: Evidence from a University Debating Competition
items.abstract: Research on Generative AI (GenAI) and work reports both productivity-compressing and inequality-expanding effects, leaving open a central question for organizations: Who benefits from GenAI and on which specific tasks? I address this question through a randomized controlled trial in competitive university debating, where participants are randomly assigned access to GenAI. Although most previous experimental work examines the impact of GenAI on written activities and across individuals, this setting allows me to study the impact of GenAI on a knowledge-intensive spoken activity and to identify heterogeneous effects across subtasks. I find that GenAI expands performance inequality in this setting. Consistent with recent theories on GenAI and work, results show that high-ability participants experience significantly larger gains from GenAI usage than their lower-ability counterparts in judgment-intensive subtasks, whereas lower-ability individuals only improve their performance in less expert components of debating, where GenAI can be used as a substitute. If these inequality-expanding effects generalize to similar spoken settings where complex ideas must be internalized and explained, rather than simply written, they would have important implications for understanding the impact of GenAI on work and inequality. This paper was accepted by Maria Guadalupe, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01063 .

items.title: When trust becomes risk: The dark side of AI-assisted financial decision-making
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in financial decision-making, raising questions about how users’ trust and perceptions of algorithmic bias relate to behavioural vulnerability. This study examines the relationships among perceived algorithmic bias, trust in AI, perceived decision-making error risk, and AI-assisted risk-taking tendency, while investigating the moderating role of perceived human oversight. Using survey data from 252 respondents analysed through partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM), the findings show that perceived algorithmic bias is positively associated with perceived decision-making error risk but is not significantly associated with trust in AI. Trust in AI is positively associated with both perceived decision-making error risk and AI-assisted risk-taking tendency. Perceived decision-making error risk is also positively associated with AI-assisted risk-taking tendency and provides a significant indirect pathway linking perceived algorithmic bias to this tendency. However, the indirect pathway through trust in AI is not statistically supported. Although the interaction between perceived human oversight and perceived algorithmic bias is statistically significant, the conditional effects at low, mean, and high levels of perceived oversight are not significant. These findings challenge the assumption that trust in AI is uniformly beneficial and highlight the distinction between trust, perceived decision-making error risk, and AI-assisted risk-taking tendency. The study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of behavioural vulnerability in AI-assisted financial decision-making and underscores the importance of transparent AI-supported recommendations, critical user evaluation, and meaningful human review.

items.title: Which Matters More for Academic Performance: Motivation or Positive Thinking?
items.abstract: This study used a cross-sectional research design to examine how motivation and positive thinking, both separately and together, are related to academic performance. A total of 340 sixteen-year-old students were randomly selected from a secondary school in Selangor, Malaysia. Motivation was measured using the 16-item Motivation Assessment Questionnaire (MAQ), which covers four dimensions: intrinsic motivation, extrinsic motivation, goal orientation and self-efficacy. Positive thinking was measured using the 12-item Positive Thinking Assessment Scale (PTAS), which covers three dimensions: optimism, resilience and self-affirmation. The results showed a strong positive relationship between motivation and positive thinking (ρ = .768, p < .001). Both motivation and positive thinking had significant positive relationships with academic performance (β = .413 and .435, respectively; p < .001). Together, they explained 63.5% of the differences in students’ academic performance. However, the difference between their two regression coefficients was not statistically significant (p = .820). Among the seven dimensions, only extrinsic motivation (β = .318, p < .005) and self-affirmation (β = .312, p < .001) had significant relationships with academic performance when all seven dimensions were examined together. The study also examined two mediation models (Positive Thinking → Motivation → Academic Performance and Motivation → Positive Thinking → Academic Performance). The indirect relationships for the two models were .317 and .334, respectively, and the difference between them was not statistically significant (p > .05). Overall, the findings do not show that either motivation or positive thinking is a stronger predictor or mediator than the other. Instead, both are related to academic performance and provide useful information that is partly shared and partly unique to each.

items.title: Who Will Conduct Science? Researchers’ Expectations of AI Capabilities and the Future of Scientific Work
items.abstract: Recent advances in generative AI systems have demonstrated their potential to outperform humans in conducting research and in answering previously unsolved scientific problems. As AI systems become increasingly capable of performing research independently, the question shifts from how researchers should use AI to how much human resources will be required in scientific research and where. We surveyed researchers worldwide about their perspectives on AI-driven scientific research, prompted by OpenAI’s bulk release of mathematical solutions in October 2026. We received over 4,000 responses from researchers across 126 countries and a wide range of disciplines. Most respondents (62%) expected AI systems to be capable of conducting research tasks independently within three years, although expectations regarding the quality of AI-generated research varied, with 41% anticipating quality comparable to or exceeding that of competent human researchers. Respondents generally supported allowing AI to assume most roles in scientific research (each with a minimum of 48%), mainly under human supervision. AI developments made one-third of respondents concerned about their own job security; mathematicians and statisticians anticipated the greatest effects on their research and careers (45%), and researchers in the humanities and arts the least (30%). Despite concerns about potential negative career consequences, respondents overwhelmingly (74%) expected AI-driven research to accelerate scientific progress. Although the limitations of this survey restrict the generalizability of its findings, the results offer an overview of how researchers across more than a hundred countries perceive rapid advances in AI. They also highlight the need to monitor AI’s impact on the scientific workforce and inform policies that support the sustainable integration of AI into scientific research.

items.title: Work design in digital platform labor: Development and validation of the Microworking Conditions Scale
items.abstract: In light of the rise of AI, microwork is becoming an increasingly important branch of the platform economy. This global labor market of individual workers who label data and moderate content supports the development of technological innovation. Little is known about their working conditions and how these conditions affect their well-being, however. This article presents three studies that outline the development of an integrative framework of working conditions in microwork, a complementary scale, and the validation of this scale. Based on current literature on microwork and guided by Self-Determination Theory (SDT), the Microworking Conditions Scale (MWCS) comprises 15 working conditions, nine adopted from existing frameworks (e.g., Work Autonomy) and six newly conceptualized (e.g., Availability Requirement). The measurement structure of the MWCS was confirmed by exploratory factor analyses ( n = 407) and confirmatory factor analysis ( n = 455). All 15 microworking conditions show convergent, discriminant, criterion, and predictive validity. The final scale consists of 45 items, three per microworking condition. The MWCS addresses the fragmented nature of the literature on microworking conditions and fills in gaps in the measurement of new working conditions emerging from microwork. The article further discusses the theoretical and practical implications, as well as directions for future research.

items.title: (No) Separation of Concerns: Philosophical Concerns about Agent Ethics and Implications for SE Practitioners
items.abstract: The use of AI agents in software engineering (SE) are commonplace, with differing levels of autonomy, a myriad of capabilities, and ability to perform a variety of tasks. Philosophers have begun to examine the ethics of such agents, and SE researchers or practitioners could benefit from them; on the other hand, SE practitioners currently explore most of these concerns through the lens of principlism. We bridge this gap by reviewing the philosophical literature on AI agents indexed in PhilPapers, and translating its ethical concerns into a research agenda for SE researchers and into implications for teams that use coding agents. A systematic mapping study of PhilPapers -- a major philosophy index and open access archive -- yielded 33 peer-reviewed papers by professional philosophers published since 2023. We coded these papers thematically, with cross-disciplinary review of the emerging themes, resulting in eight themes and 85 codes. From these, we derive seven research questions for SE, covering developers' reliance on agents, responsibility for agent-written code, ethical constraints in agent configurations, and benchmark design. For practitioners, we derive five implications: decide which choices an agent must refer to a human, keep agent-written pull requests small enough to review, pair configuration-file instructions with checks, watch for changes to tests, and record who approved what. We argue that ethical concerns cannot be separated from SE concerns into a module of their own: they arise inside code review, configuration, evaluation, and requirements work, and addressing them requires cross-disciplinary work.

items.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Multi-Agent Systems Through a Layered Taxonomy Spanning Science, Engineering, and Applications
items.abstract: Multi-agent systems have emerged as a dominant architectural paradigm for applied AI, yet deploying them effectively requires bridging scientific understanding of agent coordination with engineering constraints and real-world application demands. This survey presents a unified perspective on the multi-agent AI landscape, synthesizing research across the science of how multiple LLM-driven agents coordinate, the engineering of systems that implement that coordination under production constraints, and the application-level evidence of where such systems deliver measurable value. We introduce a layered taxonomy of multi-agent capabilities, spanning Agent Primitives, Coordination, Communication, Intelligence, and Assurance. We then organize 13 functionalities into 8 key concepts derived inductively from the literature, situated within the layered taxonomy of multi-agent capabilities: (Agent specialization, Orchestration patterns, Decision making, Context engineering, Learning, Evaluation, Tracing & Monitoring, and Security & Safety). For each concept, we trace its intellectual origins, survey current scientific findings, examine engineering design patterns, and ground the discussion in enterprise deployments. We motivate multi-agent architectures through an analysis of single-agent limitations (including context saturation, instruction-following degradation, tool selection noise, and limited modularity) while acknowledging that multi-agent decomposition is not universally superior and introduces its own coordination overhead. We identify principled criteria for when multi-agent coordination is justified over single-agent designs, and examine the responsible AI mechanisms necessary for trustworthy operation at scale. We conclude by outlining directions for future research on open challenges, including evaluation difficulty, cost efficiency, emergent security threats, and governance in a rapidly shifting regulatory landscape.

items.title: A Discussion of Community Diplomacy among Heterogeneous Human–AI Collectives
items.abstract: Who should represent a human–AI community depends on its institutional strategy, the proposed act, and the relations through which authority and practical competence are constituted. This paper connects representative selection, collective-position formation, external recognition, and continuing cooperation. It distinguishes constituencies, appointing bodies, holders, resource controllers, counterparties, and affected parties. A standard categorical pullback describes the conjunction of internal appointment and counterpart acceptance where required. Constructed constitutional histories and a standard judgment-aggregation countercase show how similar capabilities and consistent constituent judgments can support different arrangements and public positions. Agents can recognize attributed histories and selected norm derivations, acknowledge a documented contribution, and undertake bounded obligations through an authorized procedure. An archive encounter preserves plural origin narratives while enabling a restricted review and an agent’s liaison appointment. A standard proof-path functor describes replay under accepted translations and premises. Historical truth, situated interpretation, normative standing, and an operative undertaking retain distinct grounds. A further case negotiates incompatible public-audit and source-confidentiality requirements through a scoped accommodation. Its continuation examines registry standard changes, authority to hear objections, disconnection, and succession after exit. Recognition and interoperability thus become relations whose governing interfaces can themselves be contested and revised. The analysis also develops commitment stages, resource reservation, revocation, and archival continuity. Primary engagement with representation, configurable governance, recognition theory, electronic institutions, AI delegation, institutional economics, and standards supplies antecedents. Selected empirical studies locate federated governance frictions and asymmetries within their observed settings. The proposed contribution connects collective voice and continuing reception to heterogeneous epistemic means, distributed controllers, and plural institutions. Conditional mathematical results and finite diagnostics retain their assumptions. Observation and later implementation can assess effects on cooperation, human presence, answerability, and opportunities to revise a relation.

items.title: A Discussion of Responsibility, Standing, and Remedy in Human–AI Communities
items.abstract: Human–AI communities combine brief contributions with continuing projects, shared resources, and consequential undertakings. This paper develops remedial continuity as a way to investigate whether a live claim can reach an authorized and practically meaningful response through institutional change. A comparative jurisprudential inquiry connects relational powers, plural normative orders, collective identity, resource rights, evidence, and access to remedy. Selected primary legal and philosophical sources retain their jurisdictions, statuses, and argumentative scopes. Developed cases distinguish an operational actor from a represented party, operation-specific responsibility from a whole delegation chain, and claim recognition from the beneficiary and authority of a response. Human interests, protective conduct rules, and possible direct AI claims require their respective grounds. A typed route diagnostic identifies the relevant party, competent forum, lawfully usable evidence, and feasible response. Standard conditional constructions examine transition, archival answerability, jointly feasible schedules, and irreversible response order. A sustained cross-community conflict shows how historical recognition and a successful bounded agreement can coexist with contested permissions, excluded agency questions, external claims, and funding gaps. Further comparisons follow exploitation allegations, translated complaints, shared control, community splits, and continuing duties through changing operational carriers. The framework preserves configurable constitutions and context-sensitive strategies while making the effects of those choices assessable. Its contribution is a specified comparative research architecture and conditional diagnostics; implemented inquiry, independent normative criticism, and jurisdiction-specific analysis are needed to evaluate particular arrangements.

items.title: A Risk-Adaptive Trust and Safety Governance Framework for AI-Enabled Online Platforms: An Advanced Methodology for Identifying, Measuring, and Mitigating Digital Harm
items.abstract: The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into online platforms has created significant trust and safety challenges because AI systems can generate, amplify and distribute digital harms across different platform functions and stages of the AI lifecycle.This study develops a Risk-Adaptive Trust and Safety Governance Framework for AI-Enabled Online Platforms as a methodology for identifying, measuring, prioritising and mitigating digital harm.A systematic literature review and conceptual framework-development design was adopted.Relevant literature published between 2017 and 2024 was examined across major academic databases and authoritative sources, with attention given to AI-enabled digital harms, their determinants, risk assessment, risk classification, platform governance and mitigation strategies.The analysis indicates that AI-enabled digital harm is not limited to technical errors or harmful content but can emerge through data practices, model design, deployment conditions, algorithmic ranking, recommendation, moderation, personalisation and organisational decisions.The study further establishes that effective risk assessment requires multidimensional indicators that consider likelihood, severity, exposure, scale, vulnerability and contextual conditions rather than relying exclusively on technical performance measures.On this basis, the proposed framework connects five interrelated processes: identification of digital harm, examination of its determinants, measurement of risk, classification and prioritisation, and proportionate trust and safety mitigation.The framework adopts a continuous feedback approach in which risk assessment informs intervention and the outcomes of intervention generate evidence for subsequent reassessment.The study concludes that effective AI platform governance requires adaptive, evidence-based and accountable trust and safety mechanisms capable of responding to changing technologies, user behaviour and emerging forms of digital harm.

items.title: Agentic AI for Autonomous Detection and Resolution of Hold Transactions in Integrated Multi-Vendor Hospital Pharmacy Systems
items.abstract: This paper presents an agentic artificial intelligence framework that detects, diagnoses and resolves hold transactions, which are stuck or failed transactions, in integrated hospital pharmacy environments. Large health systems often run order entry, medication processing, billing, stock and inventory, laboratory, blood bank and automated dispensing software from different vendors, and holds arise at the interfaces where no single vendor sees the whole transaction. Analysts resolve holds manually today, so backlogs build up and stock records drift from physical reality. The research problem is how to automate the repetitive part of this work without weakening audit, inventory accuracy or patient safety. Using a design science approach, the paper develops a taxonomy of five hold causes, a five agent architecture based on a monitor, analyze, plan, execute and knowledge control loop, a tiered autonomy policy with approval gated reprocessing, and an artificial intelligence governance model. A 30 day simulation with 20 replications and a sensitivity analysis evaluate the design. Under stated assumptions, about 82 percent of holds are resolved automatically and mean handling time falls from about 43 to 11 minutes, but the human escalation queue stays bounded only above a break even of about 80 percent automatic resolution. The work indicates that governed agentic automation is a promising option for multivendor hospital pharmacy operations, provided that automatic resolution and false fix rates are confirmed through the staged pilot protocol proposed here.
