items.title: Agentic AI in education: design logic, evidence quality, and theoretical foundations
items.abstract: Introduction Agentic artificial intelligence systems in education represent a qualitative departure from traditional educational technology. Unlike reactive tools requiring continuous human direction, agentic AI monitors learner states, initiates interventions without requests, and pursues pedagogical objectives independently. Yet this technical sophistication has outpaced theoretical development, leaving fundamental questions unaddressed: How does agent autonomy affect learner agency? When does proactive support enhance versus undermine self-directed learning? What theories adequately address systems demonstrating independent goal pursuit? Methods This study analyzes recent agentic AI research using the ADO-TCM (Antecedents-Decisions-Outcomes-Theories-Contexts-Methods) framework, which traces design logic from problem identification through decisions to outcomes while assessing theoretical grounding, contextual boundaries, and methodological rigor. Following PRISMA guidelines, three researchers independently coded the titles and abstracts of 170 primary studies, achieving substantial agreement. Results As reported in titles and abstracts, the field is characterized by theoretical absence rather than diversity: the vast majority of papers engage no learning theory and invoke AI capabilities as rationale without engaging learning sciences foundations. Alongside this absence, most abstracts do not report whether agents operate autonomously or under supervision, papers addressing multiple problems more often bundle several pedagogical roles in one agent, and most abstracts report outcomes without comparison groups. Because coding was based on titles and abstracts, these gaps describe reported information and require full-text examination before they can be attributed to the underlying research. Discussion Existing theories (e.g., zone of proximal development, cognitive load theory, self-determination theory, activity theory) inadequately address agentic AI's autonomous characteristics. Scaffolding anticipation, autonomy load, and distributed autonomy are offered as conceptual propositions for extending them. We propose theoretical directions, evidence standards, and equity-centered principles to advance agentic AI research from atheoretical demonstration toward theoretically grounded, methodologically rigorous, and equitably distributed practice.

items.title: AGI and Education 5.0: A Systematic Review of AGI-Driven Sustainable Education Across the Learning Lifespan
items.abstract: Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) is increasingly envisioned as a transformative force in education, yet research on AGI-driven education remains fragmented across educational stages and rarely incorporates sustainability into system design and evaluation. This systematic review examines how AGI and large language model (LLM)/generative AI technologies reshape education across the learning lifespan and how sustainability can be embedded in AGI-powered education. Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and Google Scholar for studies published between 2015 and 2026, using keyword groups related to general intelligence, education, and sustainability. After screening, 85 peer-reviewed studies were included and synthesized through narrative synthesis. Given that full AGI remains unrealized, current LLM and generative AI systems are treated as emergent approximations of AGI’s educational potential. We develop an organizing framework that maps AGI’s transformative roles, key mechanisms, and sustainability implications across early childhood, K–12, higher education, and lifelong learning. The review identifies four emerging application scenarios and introduces a multidimensional sustainability lens encompassing cognitive, economic, social, and ethical–environmental dimensions, extending evaluation beyond conventional academic performance indicators. It also highlights persistent technical, social, and ethical challenges. By integrating stage-specific transformations with a lifespan and sustainability perspective, this review provides a reference and research agenda for the responsible and sustainable integration of AGI into Education 5.0.

items.title: Agricultural operations centers and data-driven management in the sugarcane sector: foundations for the design of operational procedures and their impacts
items.abstract: The mechanization of sugarcane harvesting and the spread of digital technologies in the field have increased the amount of data available on machines, trucks and agricultural operations, which has favored the creation of agricultural operations centers dedicated to real-time monitoring of field crews. This article, based on a narrative review of scientific, technical and regulatory literature, discusses the foundations that should guide the design and use of operational procedures in these centers, as well as their expected impacts. The analysis brings together contributions from digital agriculture, agricultural machinery engineering, harvest and transport logistics, cognitive ergonomics, decision theory and studies on workplace monitoring. The results indicate that the value of an operations center depends less on the amount of data collected and more on the quality of data recording, the definition of indicators consistent with the actual losses of the system, clarity about who decides and within what time frame, the handling of alarms and the integration of analysis routines into the continuous improvement cycle. It is concluded that well-structured procedures can convert connectivity and telemetry into operational, safety and sustainability gains, provided they are accompanied by data governance, transparency with workers and systematic evaluation of results.

items.title: AI-Assisted Desk Verification of Sentinel-2 Training Samples for Coastal Land Cover Mapping
items.abstract: Supervised land cover mapping of a historical baseline needs reference labels that can no longer be collected in the field. This study documents and evaluates a desk verification workflow that produced Sentinel-2 training samples for a 2019–2020 baseline map of the Lima Puluh coastal landscape, Batu Bara, North Sumatra (about 24,300 ha), where oil palm, paddy, mangrove and aquaculture ponds meet. Candidate points were generated in Google Earth Engine from rule-based frames in two rounds. A multimodal large language model proposed a label and a structured note for each candidate from very-high-resolution basemap chips and Sentinel-2 2019–2020 chips, and the researcher reviewed every proposal. Of 1,114 candidates, 1,024 were reviewed; 450 were confirmed, 364 rejected and 210 left uncertain. A 100 m within-class spacing rule gave 434 training points in seven classes. Frame precision ranged from 0% for index-only water masks to 98% for map-anchored settlement frames. In the priority review of 64 uncertain water and pond points, 58 were excluded, mainly because of mixed land–water pixels, ambiguous fallow plots and water that appeared after 2019; the researcher overrode 1 of 64 proposals. Targeted additions of oil palm and coastal paddy points raised spatially cross-validated kappa from 0.823 to 0.860 and, on a blind validation sample of 300 points, overall accuracy from 0.850 to 0.873 and paddy producer’s accuracy from 0.709 to 0.846. AI-assisted desk verification can supply auditable training data when field access is impossible, provided that a human decides every label and accuracy is estimated independently.

items.title: AI-assisted virtual patient simulation and communication self-efficacy in healthcare professions students: a randomized pilot study
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare systems is transforming not only clinical practice but also the educational pathways preparing future healthcare professionals. This pilot study examines the pedagogical use of AI-assisted conversational simulation in healthcare professions education, comparing AI-based virtual patient interaction with traditional role-play. A randomized parallel-group pilot study with a post-test-only design involved 56 students enrolled in the Master's Degree Program in Diagnostic Technical Healthcare Professions at the University of Foggia. Participants were randomly assigned, through stratified randomization with permuted blocks, to AI-assisted communication training (Group A, n = 28) or traditional role-play with human facilitators (Group B, n = 28) in 1:1 allocation. The 20-hour educational intervention integrated Medical Humanities, healthcare communication, experiential learning, and simulation-based education; Group A trained with a publicly available custom GPT virtual patient using the voice mode of ChatGPT Plus. Communication self-efficacy (SE-12), the primary outcome, was significantly higher in Group A (mean difference 5.74, 95% CI 3.08–8.40; Cohen's d = 1.18, 95% CI 0.60–1.76), an effect that persisted after adjusting for prior AI experience. Communication apprehension (PRCA-24), the secondary outcome, did not differ significantly between groups, either overall or on any of the four subscales. These preliminary findings suggest that AI-assisted conversational simulation may usefully complement traditional communication training and contribute to the broader debate on digital literacy in health professions curricula. The post-test-only design, the single assessment at 7 days, and the use of a non-validated Italian translation of the SE-12 limit inference about causality and durability.

items.title: AI-Driven Digital Transformation: Reconfiguring the Organization While Remaining Responsive to Emergent Risk
items.abstract: A challenge for organizations is that AI-driven digital transformation introduces both unseen and unprecedented risk. From a systems perspective, such risk develops between formal constraints and situated practice; organizational members must interpret AI outputs in context and determine whether to accept, modify, or override them. Risk becomes more apparent when outputs are unexpected, system behavior is difficult to explain, or experience with existing tools raises concerns. Such interactions among organizational members and AI systems serve as a form of distributed sensing, whereby indications of risk are detected and interpreted jointly and iteratively rather than through centralized monitoring. The growing prevalence of generative and agentic AI makes this capacity relevant to organizations, as members initiate actions with AI systems under conditions that cannot be fully specified in advance. AI-driven digital transformation therefore calls for organizations to maintain ongoing interpretation and adjustment, enabling them to balance control with coordinated, adaptive action while remaining responsive to emergent risks.

items.title: AI-Driven Emotion Recognition and Decision-Making in Mental Health: Ethical and Psychological Implications for Early Detection and Human-Computer Interaction
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being integrated across various fields. AI advancements have catalyzed a paradigm shift in psychological assessment and intervention, aiming to rapidly transform how mental health and psychological imbalance are assessed, monitored, and treated. In this research, we examine the role of AI in the early detection of affective and cognitive disorders, with a focus on depression, anxiety, and stress-related psychopathologies using emotion recognition technologies and predictive modeling. We explore how affective computing techniques such as facial expression analysis, speech recognition, and natural language processing are integrated within digital mental health platforms for efficient therapeutic alliance, accurate clinical decision-making, and boosted user engagement. In addition, this research investigates the effects of human-computer interaction in an AI-powered mental health context, addressing constructs such as user trust, engagement, and cognitive reliance on autonomous systems. A critical analysis of ethical and governance factors demonstrated several pitfalls that hinder AI-driven mental health adoption. These include algorithm opacity and bias, non-compliance with regulatory frameworks and data protection policies, and inequitable access to existing platforms. The interdisciplinary synthesis employed in this study provides evidence-based insight with strategic recommendations for developing, deploying, and regulating AI-driven mental health solutions in healthcare systems.

items.title: AI-Generated Code Issues: A Taxonomy from Repository Histories, AI Conversations, and Developer Interviews
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate source code, yet the quality issues in such code remain only partially understood. Understanding these issues can help developers adapt quality assurance practices, such as code review and testing, to better detect problems that may be more common in AI-generated than in human-written code. We study how quality issues in AI-generated code manifest in real software development activities through a mixed-method empirical study that draws on evidence from three complementary sources. First, we mine GitHub commits whose messages explicitly attribute a fix to a problem in AI-generated code, and we manually inspect the 914 matched commits to remove false positives and classify the quality issue being corrected. Second, we collect developers' shared conversations with AI tools, identify conversations including source code and textual signals of model mistakes, and manually analyze 299 of them to classify the underlying quality issue. Third, we interview 20 practitioners and researchers who use AI coding tools to enrich and validate the obtained catalog of quality issues. From these analyses, we derive a taxonomy of 87 types of developer-attributed quality issues in AI-generated code, going beyond functional bugs. Our findings contribute an empirically grounded taxonomy and implications for the design and evaluation of AI coding assistants and agents.
